b: Whether you’re getting ready to host, scrambling to choose an appetizer to bring to your family celebration, laying low at home, or gearing up to travel, gratitude is probably top (or near top) of mind. We all know what the season is about, but the truth is, it might be hitting differently for you this year. Maybe things have been tense with your spouse lately, or you’re in the midst of a hard season. Perhaps you know you could be better at expressing gratitude year round. Or maybe you’re searching for ways to put a grateful mindset into action. Everyone needs different things at different times to feel encouraged and inspired. So we’ve pulled together some of our posts on gratitude to help you find the exact thing you need to read today.

Some days, gratitude comes easily. Other days, it can feel forced, fake, or like your heart’s just not in it. If you’re in the second camp, this is the post for you. It explores gratitude as a muscle you strengthen with practice rather than a feeling you have (or don’t). It walks through simple habits like noticing the small, everyday things and taking a moment to thank your spouse with your full attention.
Try it tomorrow: Pick one ordinary thing your spouse does that you usually don’t think about, and give them a heartfelt thank you.
When things have been snippy and tense

If you and your spouse already seem irritated with each other lately, the holidays have the potential to exacerbate that. Packed schedules, complicated family dynamics, and seasonal stressors put extra pressure on both of you, and you might be taking it out on each other. This post explains how gratitude helps prevent small frustrations from turning into big arguments. It covers how appreciation builds a cycle of positive interactions, how it helps you see the whole person instead of one irritating moment, and how it tempers resentment before it sets in.
Try it tomorrow: If you find yourself getting annoyed with your spouse, take a second to ask yourself what good intention might be behind the action that’s getting on your nerves.
When things have been hard, and you feel guilty for not being more thankful

This post is for anyone who might be carrying something heavy this season: a loss, financial stress, a strained relationship, or just an exhausting year. It makes the case that gratitude doesn’t cancel out other feelings – you don’t have to pretend you’re fine to be thankful for the good things. It also offers a small language shift that makes a big difference: swapping “but” for “and.”
Try it tomorrow: If someone asks what you’re grateful for, it’s okay to be honest and say both parts: “It’s been a hard year, and I’m grateful we’ve gotten through it together.”
When you want to turn gratitude into something more

Gratitude often manifests as a feeling, but it can be put into action, too. This post offers ways you and your spouse can do it as a team and what happens when you do: connecting over shared values, modeling generosity for the people around you, gaining a meaningful shared activity, and sparking positive feelings that carry over into your marriage.
Try it tomorrow: Come up with one idea for giving back that speaks to you, and commit to seeing it through, even if it’s after the holidays.
When you want a quick way to connect with your spouse

Turn your feelings of gratitude into a moment of connection amidst the holiday hustle with these three prompts: something small you noticed this year, something hard you’re still grateful for, and something you appreciate about each other that you haven’t said in a while.
Try it tomorrow: Before family arrives or the kitchen gets busy, take five minutes to sit down and answer these questions with your spouse to center yourselves on what truly matters.

Whatever your Thanksgiving looks like this year, we hope one of these posts resonated, and you get a chance to tell your spouse how much you appreciate them. You don’t need to prepare an eloquent speech; it’s the heart that counts.
